title: Despite diverse talk, Roman doctors agree with the Councils: images are owed cult and ‘adoration,’ with bow, kiss, incense, and lights as legitimate signs
source_text: XXXII. Itaque Doctores Ecclesiae Romanae, utut paulum diverse loquantur, de his tamen, quae sunt ab istius Ecclesiae Conciliis sancita & definita, inter se consentiunt. Primo, scilicet, imagines non ad simplicem commemorationem, in templis habendas & retinendas esse, sed imaginibus Christi, & Beatae Virginis, ac aliorum etiam sanctorum, aliquem cultum & honorem deberi, & merito posse tribui. Secundo honorem illum voce adorationis recte & bono sensu exprimi posse. Tertio reverentiae & submissionis signa, quae imaginibus illis exhibentur eas apertione capitis salutando, item eas osculando, genu coram illis flectendo, ac denique incense & luminaria offerendo, honoris illius esse notas legitimas, & minime culpandas.
pass_a_gloss: Therefore the Doctors of the Roman Church, however diversely they speak a little, yet among themselves agree on those things which have been sanctioned and defined by that Church’s Councils. First, namely, that images are not to be had and kept in temples for simple commemoration, but that some cult and honor are owed to the images of Christ and of the Blessed Virgin and of other saints also, and can deservedly be attributed. Second, that that honor can rightly and in a good sense be expressed by the word adoration. Third, that the signs of reverence and submission which are exhibited to those images—by saluting them with uncovering of the head, likewise by kissing them, by bending the knee before them, and finally by offering incense and lights—are legitimate marks of that honor and by no means to be blamed.
pass_b_english: Beneath the quarrel, Roman doctors lock step with the Councils on three points: images are for cult not bare memory; ‘adoration’ is a fair name; bare head, kiss, kneel, incense, and lights are lawful honor-signs.

choices.why: Cultic use, not mnemonic décor alone.
